clean_story:
Virtual copies. Real-world mirrors.
The term digital twin comes from the idea of a perfect, living replica of a physical object, updated in real time.

A factory’s engine may seem static, but its digital twin hums with data—temperature, vibration, wear—like a shadow that moves before the object does. Sensors feed the twin, which predicts failures before they happen. In 2016, Siemens used a digital twin to optimize a gas turbine, cutting downtime by 50 percent. No guesswork. Just math and motion. A city’s traffic lights can have twins too, adjusting flows in real time to ease congestion. The twin doesn’t replace the original; it makes it sharper. Three related subjects are predictive maintenance, virtual simulations and smart cities.
